verses.note: Humanity alone is made after divine deliberation and in God's image. The verse defines human beings by their relation to God before anything else, and gives them a vocation: to represent God's rule over the world he made.

Man and woman bear God's image equally. Whatever else the image means, it cannot be restricted to one sex, one people, or one class, and the New Testament grounds respect for every person in it (James 3:9).
Dominion is exercised as God's image-bearers, so it has to reflect his character. Psalm 8 marvels at this calling, and Hebrews 2:5-9 says it finds its true fulfillment in Jesus.

Nefesh here is not the immortal soul of Greek philosophy but the whole living creature, made of earth and animated by God. The verse holds together frailty and dignity: dust, and yet breathed into by God. How body and soul relate, and what survives death, is taught elsewhere in Scripture and confessed by the church (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23), and the final hope is bodily resurrection.

Even in a perfect garden with God present, human beings are not made to be solitary. Relationship with other people belongs to the goodness of creation, and isolation is a lack God himself names and meets.

God lets the man's naming stand. Human decisions have real weight in God's world: the dominion of 1:28 is exercised here by speech that orders and classifies, a first picture of human culture and science under God.

The man recognizes in the woman not a possession but a kinswoman of his own substance. Human sexual difference is presented as correspondence and delight, the first human speech in the Bible a cry of recognition.

Human beings remain dust, bound to the earth they came from. The New Testament's hope does not deny this but answers it with resurrection: the body sown in weakness is raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42-49).

The first murder is the killing of a brother. Scripture treats every murder in that light: 9:6 grounds the prohibition of murder in the image of God, and Jesus traces murder back to anger and contempt toward a brother (Matthew 5:21-22).
Genesis restates human dignity at the head of a list of deaths. The fall has not revoked the likeness of God or the blessing of 1:28; the genealogy is how the blessing to multiply goes on working.

The image of God is passed on through ordinary human birth, which is why Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 can treat every later person as bearing it. Many interpreters add that Adam also passes on the fallen condition of chapter 3, a point Christian traditions develop differently in their teaching on original sin.

The human vocation given at creation survives the flood. Humanity's calling to fill the earth was not cancelled by sin or by judgment, which is why the Old Testament can go on to treat children and fruitfulness as gifts of God's blessing.

The image of God is not lost after the flood. Genesis 9:6 speaks of every human being, the violent ones included, as still made in God's image, and it grounds the gravity of murder there. James 3:9 makes the same argument about cursing people made in God's likeness.
Every nation descends from one family that came out of the ark. Paul makes the same point before the council of the Areopagus in Athens: God made every nation of men from one man (Acts 17:26).

Peoples at the far edge of Israel's world, horse riders from the north and Greeks across the sea, are named as members of Noah's family. Later prophets place several of them in visions of the end (Ezekiel 38:2-6; Isaiah 66:19), but here they are simply kin.

Ham's line includes Egypt, Babylon, and the Canaanites, Israel's greatest oppressors and rivals, and it is described with exactly the same words as the others. The table does not rank the three branches; each has its clans, languages, lands, and nations.

Joktan's descendants are as much Shem's children as Peleg's, yet the story will not follow them. Descent from Shem does not by itself put a people in the line of promise, and the table gives the side branch as much care as any other.
Humanity begins as one people with one speech. The unity itself is not condemned; the story will show that the problem lies in what united humanity sets out to do with it.

The equation of blood and life belongs to Scripture's wider view of living beings as embodied. Life is not treated as a separate spark hidden inside the body but as bound up with the flesh and blood God made.
Joy in God is not only inward; it includes the body. The psalm's hope is for the whole person, and the mention of flesh anticipates the bodily resurrection the New Testament will proclaim.
Contempt can strip a person of their humanity in others' eyes, and the sufferer feels it. The psalm will answer that God has not despised the afflicted (verse 24), using the same verb.
Scripture describes suffering in bodily terms: bones, heart, inward parts. The psalm treats the body as part of the person who suffers and who will be restored, not as a shell to be escaped.

Human frailty is stated without contempt. Grass is beautiful and brief, and so are we. Psalm 103:15-17 draws the same contrast between human days like grass and the LORD's steadfast love from everlasting to everlasting.

Ezekiel's diagnosis is that the problem is inward and total: not a few bad acts but a heart turned to stone. The remedy has to be as deep as the problem, which is why the promise speaks of a transplant rather than a treatment.

The vision follows the order of Genesis 2:7, where God first forms the man from dust and then breathes life into him. A body without God's breath is not yet a living person. Scripture treats human life as body and breath together, both from God.
‘Are you not much more valuable than they?’ assumes a distinct human worth under God, echoing the image of God in Genesis 1:26-28.
The verse sets a limit on human capacity without condemning human nature. What people are by birth, even good and religious people, cannot bring them into the life of God.

The appeal to what is natural grounds Paul's sexual ethic in creation rather than in custom alone, in the traditional reading, while revisionist readers argue that his idea of nature is shaped by ancient assumptions. Churches remain divided on how the verses apply today, as the chapter note sets out.

Conscience is part of human nature as created: every person carries an inner witness that the moral law is real. Paul elsewhere shows it can be weak (1 Corinthians 8:7) or seared (1 Timothy 4:2), so it is a real but fallible witness.

Humanity is one, bound together in its origin and its condition. Paul's thought depends on solidarity: the act of one representative can shape the destiny of many, which is exactly what makes Christ's act for the many intelligible.

The ‘I’ that begins here is one of the most debated figures in the Bible. The main readings are autobiography (Paul recalling his own experience), Adam (the first man meeting the first command), Israel (the nation receiving the law at Sinai), and a representative ‘I’ standing for anyone under the law. Werner Georg Kümmel's Römer 7 und die Bekehrung des Paulus (1929) argued that the ‘I’ is a rhetorical form and not autobiography, and his view reshaped modern study. Ernst Käsemann heard Adam most clearly in verses 7-13; Douglas Moo, in his commentary (New International Commentary, 1996), reads Paul speaking in solidarity with Israel at Sinai; many hold that Paul's own experience and Adam's story are both present.

Read with Adam in view, the verses retell Genesis 2-3: a man alive in God's presence, a single command, sin's entrance, and death. Read as Israel, they tell of Sinai, where the law given for life (Leviticus 18:5) became, through sin, a ministry of death (2 Corinthians 3:7). On any reading the verses show that knowing the command does not give the power to keep it.

The question of the present-tense ‘I’ divides faithful readers. The early Greek interpreters, and Augustine in his early work on Romans (the Propositions, about 394), held that Paul spoke for a person under the law, not a Christian. Augustine later changed his mind, in his writings against the Pelagians (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, about 421) and his Retractations, concluding that ‘I delight in God's law’ (verse 22) could be said only by a renewed person; Luther (Lectures on Romans, 1515-1516), who saw here the believer at once righteous and sinner, and Calvin (commentary, 1540) followed, as did C. E. B. Cranfield and James Dunn, who reads the passage as the tension of a believer living between the ages. Jacobus Arminius wrote a treatise defending the pre-conversion reading; John Wesley saw a person awakened by the law but not yet freed; Kümmel (1929), Moo, and many others read it as life under the law seen in hindsight from faith.

The verses show a will that genuinely wants the good and is not able to carry it out. Whatever the identity of the ‘I’, Paul denies that right knowledge and good intentions are enough to make a person good.

‘Nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh’ is a key text for the doctrine that sin affects every part of fallen human nature, which Reformed theology calls total depravity (meaning not that people are as bad as they could be, but that no part of them is untouched). Paul still speaks of a willing self distinct from the flesh.

The ‘inner person’ who delights in God's law is the strongest evidence for the reading that Paul describes a believer; the captivity to sin's law is the strongest evidence against it. The verses leave the reader in the tension on purpose, so that the cry of verse 24 is felt.
In Paul ‘flesh’ is not the body but human existence turned away from God and closed on itself. The verses define people by what their minds are set on, not by their bodily nature.

Paul thinks of humanity as bound up with its representatives: Adam's act brought death to all his descendants, and Christ's resurrection brings life to all who belong to him. The fuller development of the pattern is Romans 5:12-21.

Paul reads human history as two beginnings, each headed by one man. Adam's life was given and could be lost; Christ's risen life is life that gives life to others. Believers belong first to the one and then to the other.

Humility is defined not as low self-regard but as regard for others: counting their good as weightier than one's own. Paul grounds this new human virtue in the pattern of Christ rather than in Greek ethics, where it had little place.
The psalm's question sets the dignity of humanity inside a frank recognition of its smallness. Humanity's worth is located in God's attention, not in size or power.

The vocation of Genesis 1:28 and Psalm 8, to rule over creation, has not failed but is unfinished. The author is realistic about the present: human beings do not now rule the world as the psalm describes.
